steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a control paper proposing a simple Nussbaum function based, PID-structured controller for tracking control of robot manipulators with unknown dynamics and unknown control direction. Cover the motivation and related approaches, what we propose, our contributions, and the paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation: robots in many industries, nonlinearities and uncertainties, advanced controllers too complex
2. PID control: simple, but limited; tuning add-ons bring complexity back
3. Unknown control direction and the Nussbaum function approach
4. Why we do this: a simple, low-complexity controller combining PID and Nussbaum
5. This work and main contributions
6. Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
   - robotic systems expanding across industries -> advanced control mechanisms (functionality, adaptability)
   - progress from rigorous mathematical frameworks, but nonlinearities + uncertainties still significant challenges
   - advanced strategies: fuzzy logic, Kalman filter, iterative learning control, actor–critic learning
   - but their complexity makes real-world application hard -> need to refine/simplify control for manipulators
2. PID control
   - intuitive design, simplicity; pillar for theory and practice in many real-world systems
   - addresses complexity issue in robotic control
   - limits: weight updating, stability assurance, extensive parameter tuning in dynamic environments
   - refinements: optimization techniques for gain tuning -> adaptability
   - but these add new complexities, undermine the simplicity
3. Unknown control direction
   - wrong gain direction can destabilize system instead of guiding it to desired state
   - methods: logic-based switching, extreme seeking, nonlinear PI control
   - Nussbaum function approach = most studied
   - effective in robotic control, but integration into full framework complicates system
   - need more accessible strategies: Nussbaum advantages w/o excessive complexity
4. Our motivation
   - simple, low-complexity strategy for unknown control gain direction in manipulators
   - PID limitations + Nussbaum complexity -> combine simple PID structure with Nussbaum function
   - ensures stability, enhances performance, inexpensive online computation; bridges the gap
5. This work
   - adaptive Nussbaum-based control; unknown dynamics and control directions
   - rooted in PID structure; simplifies yet enhances
   - closed-loop stability via direct Lyapunov analysis (unlike conventional PID)
   - automatic gain adjustment, linking parameters -> fewer tuning requirements, efficiency/response
   - contributions:
     - Nussbaum function in PID structure; simple, guarantees stability, no knowledge of robot dynamics or control direction
     - linked PID terms + adaptive laws -> automatic gains, minimal parameters, real-time use
6. Organization
   - Sec II problem formulation, preliminaries
   - Sec III Nussbaum Function-based control design + stability analysis
   - Sec IV numerical simulations
   - Sec V conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Robotic systems are being used more and more in many industries, and this has pushed the development of advanced control mechanisms to make them more functional and adaptable. There has been progress because of rigorous mathematical frameworks, but the nonlinearities and uncertainties that are part of robotic operations are still a big challenge. So advanced control strategies are needed to deal with these complexities, for example fuzzy logic, Kalman filter, iterative learning control, and actor–critic learning. But these methods are complex themselves and this often makes it hard to apply them in real-world scenarios. So research is still needed to refine and simplify the control solutions for robotic manipulators.

In control of robotic manipulators, PID control is known for being intuitive to design and simple, and so it is a pillar both for theory and for practical application in a lot of real-world systems. It deals with the common problem of complexity in robotic control strategies. But traditional PID control has limitations, especially in weight updating, in assuring stability, and in needing a lot of parameter tuning in dynamic environments. There have been attempts to refine PID control and make it more adaptable, like using optimization techniques to tune the gains. These enhancements can bring in new complexities though, which somewhat undermines the simplicity that made PID control appealing.

It is crucial in robotic system control to understand the direction of the control gain, because if it is applied incorrectly the system can be destabilized instead of being guided to the desired state. There are various methods for the unknown control direction, such as logic-based switching, extreme seeking, and nonlinear PI control, but the Nussbaum function approach is the method studied the most. Nussbaum-based strategies are effective in robotic control. However, integrating them into the whole control framework can make the overall system complicated. So it is important to develop strategies that are more accessible and use the advantages of the Nussbaum function without too much complexity in the control framework.

- need simple, low-complexity strategy for unknown control gain direction in manipulators
- PID limitations + Nussbaum complexity -> novel approach: simple PID structure + Nussbaum function
- ensures stability, enhances performance, inexpensive online computation; bridges the gap

[this work]
- adaptive Nussbaum-based control for unknown dynamics and control directions
- rooted in PID structure; simplifies yet enhances effectiveness
- closed-loop stability via direct Lyapunov analysis, unlike conventional PID
- automatic gain adjustment + linking parameters -> far fewer tuning requirements, no extra complexity
- contributions:
  - Nussbaum function in PID structure; simple, guarantees stability, no knowledge of robot dynamics or control direction
  - linked PID terms + adaptive laws -> automatic gains, minimal parameters, real-time use

[organization]
- Sec II problem formulation + preliminaries; Sec III control design + stability analysis; Sec IV numerical simulations; Sec V conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Robotic systems are being used more and more in many industries, and this has pushed the development of advanced control mechanisms to make them more functional and adaptable. There has been progress because of rigorous mathematical frameworks, but the nonlinearities and uncertainties that are part of robotic operations are still a big challenge. So advanced control strategies are needed to deal with these complexities, for example fuzzy logic, Kalman filter, iterative learning control, and actor–critic learning. But these methods are complex themselves and this often makes it hard to apply them in real-world scenarios. So research is still needed to refine and simplify the control solutions for robotic manipulators.

In control of robotic manipulators, PID control is known for being intuitive to design and simple, and so it is a pillar both for theory and for practical application in a lot of real-world systems. It deals with the common problem of complexity in robotic control strategies. But traditional PID control has limitations, especially in weight updating, in assuring stability, and in needing a lot of parameter tuning in dynamic environments. There have been attempts to refine PID control and make it more adaptable, like using optimization techniques to tune the gains. These enhancements can bring in new complexities though, which somewhat undermines the simplicity that made PID control appealing.

It is crucial in robotic system control to understand the direction of the control gain, because if it is applied incorrectly the system can be destabilized instead of being guided to the desired state. There are various methods for the unknown control direction, such as logic-based switching, extreme seeking, and nonlinear PI control, but the Nussbaum function approach is the method studied the most. Nussbaum-based strategies are effective in robotic control. However, integrating them into the whole control framework can make the overall system complicated. So it is important to develop strategies that are more accessible and use the advantages of the Nussbaum function without too much complexity in the control framework.

Because of these complexities and challenges, our research is driven by the need for a control strategy that is simple and low in complexity and that manages the unknown control gain direction in robotic manipulators, which is a critical aspect. We acknowledge the limitations of traditional PID control and that Nussbaum-based methods are complex, and we introduce a novel approach that combines the simple structure of PID control with what the Nussbaum function can do. The method ensures stability and enhances performance, and the control mechanism is inexpensive in online computational demands, so it bridges the gap in robotic control strategies that we mentioned.

In this work we present a control strategy for robotic manipulators that deals with unknown dynamics and unknown control directions with an adaptive Nussbaum-based control. The approach is based on the PID control structure, and it simplifies the control scheme but also makes it more effective. Unlike conventional PID methods, we ensure the stability of the closed-loop system with direct Lyapunov analysis. Also, the strategy has automatic gain adjustment and uses linking parameters, which reduces the number of tuning requirements a lot, and this makes the system more efficient and responsive without complicating the control framework. The main contributions are:

- We integrate the Nussbaum function into the PID structure to control robotic manipulators. The controller is simple but it guarantees stability, and it does not need knowledge of the robot dynamics or the control direction.

- We use linked PID terms and set up adaptive laws, so the controller determines the gains automatically with minimal parameter requirements, and this makes it easier to apply in real-time scenarios.

The rest of the paper is as follows. Section II is about problem formulation and preliminaries, which give the theoretical groundwork. Section III introduces the Nussbaum Function-based control design and the stability analysis. Section IV presents numerical simulations that show the control strategy is effective. Section V concludes the paper and summarizes the key findings and implications of the research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The rapid expansion of robotic systems across various industries has driven the development of advanced control mechanisms to enhance their functionality and adaptability. Despite the progress made possible by rigorous mathematical frameworks, the nonlinearities and uncertainties intrinsic to robotic operations still pose significant challenges. This highlights the need for advanced control strategies like fuzzy logic [1], Kalman filter [2], iterative learning control [3], and actor–critic learning [4] to counteract these complexities. However, the complexity of these methods often complicates their application in real-world scenarios, which is why research to refine and simplify control solutions for robotic manipulators is ongoing.

In the field of control for robotic manipulators, PID control is recognized for its intuitive design and simplicity, making it a pillar for both theoretical exploration and practical application across numerous real-world systems [5,6]. It addresses the widespread issue of complexity in robotic control strategies. However, traditional PID controls face limitations, particularly in weight updating, stability assurance, and the need for extensive parameter tuning in dynamic environments [7]. Attempts to refine PID control, such as using optimization techniques for gain tuning, aim to enhance its adaptability [8,9,10]. However, these enhancements can introduce new complexities, somewhat undermining the original appeal of PID control’s simplicity.

Understanding the direction of control gain is crucial in robotic system control, as incorrect application can destabilize the system instead of guiding it to the desired state. While various methods exist to address the unknown control direction, such as logic-based switching [11], extreme seeking [12], and nonlinear PI control [13], the Nussbaum function approach [14] is the most studied method [15,16,17,18]. Nussbaum-based strategies are effective in robotic control; however, integrating them into the comprehensive control framework can complicate the overall system. This highlights the importance of developing more accessible strategies that use the Nussbaum function’s advantages while avoiding excessive complexity in the control framework.

Given these complexities and challenges, our research is driven by the need for a control strategy that is simple and low in complexity, effectively managing the critical aspect of unknown control gain direction in robotic manipulators. Acknowledging the limitations of traditional PID controls and the complexities of Nussbaum-based methods, we introduce a novel approach that combines the simple structure of PID control with the capability of the Nussbaum function. This method ensures stability and enhances performance, offering a control mechanism that is inexpensive in online computational demands and bridging the mentioned gap in robotic control strategies.

In this work, we present a control strategy for robotic manipulators that tackles unknown dynamics and control directions through an adaptive Nussbaum-based control. Our approach, rooted in the PID control structure, simplifies yet enhances the effectiveness of the control scheme. Unlike conventional PID methods, we ensure the closed-loop system’s stability through direct Lyapunov analysis. Additionally, our strategy features automatic gain adjustment and uses linking parameters, significantly reducing the number of tuning requirements and thereby improving the system’s efficiency and response without complicating the control framework. The main contributions are as follows:

- • We integrate the Nussbaum function into the PID structure for the control of robotic manipulators. The controller is simple, yet it guarantees stability without requiring knowledge of robot dynamics or control direction.

- • By using linked PID terms and establishing adaptive laws, the controller automates gain determination with minimal parameter requirements, which facilitates its application in real-time scenarios.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows: Section II covers problem formulation and preliminaries, setting the theoretical groundwork. Section III introduces the Nussbaum Function-based control design and its stability analysis. Numerical simulations demonstrating the effectiveness of the control strategy are presented in Section IV. Section V concludes the paper, summarizing the key findings and implications of this research.
